stem:
Smita writes the prime factorisation $576 = 2^{6} \times 3^{2}$. She wants to know whether $576$ is a perfect square and, if it is, what its square root is.

Which claim is correct?

options.text: Report the words factor pair as the square root of $576$.
Finding a factor pair is what creates the prime factorisation $2^{6} \times 3^{2}$.
$576$ is a perfect square because the primes split into two identical groups $2^{3} \times 3$ and $2^{3} \times 3$, so $\sqrt{576} = 24$.
Read $576$ as a perfect cube and take its cube root instead of pairing the prime factors.

teacher.key_rationale: All exponents in 2^6×3^2 are even, so the primes pair into two groups each equal to 2^3×3=24, and √576=24. Naming factor pair, reversing factorisation and pairing, or switching to cube roots all miss the perfect-square hinge.
